title: The product owner
blurb: The iterative project role that represents users, owns and prioritises the backlog, and accepts or rejects work each iteration.
question: A gym chain is building a class-booking app in two-week time boxes. Members suddenly ask for a waiting-list feature. Who decides whether it is built next, and on what basis?

teach.h: The voice of the business in the team
teach.body: The product owner is a role used on iterative (agile) projects. The product owner represents the business and its users, owns and prioritises the product backlog (the list of requirements), clarifies requirements for the team, and accepts or rejects completed work at the end of each iteration. In plain English: the product owner decides what gets built next and whether what was built is good enough, always aiming to maximise value.

The product backlog is the prioritised list of everything the product might need: features, requirements and fixes, with the most valuable at the top. It is never 'finished'. As users give feedback after each iteration, new items are added and the order changes. The product owner owns it, so the team always knows what to work on next. Priorities are often set with MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time.

head: Rank
Backlog item

rows: Pay by card in the app

teach.caption: The product owner moved the waiting list up from rank 5 to rank 3 after members asked for it.

teach.h: The product owner in every iteration
teach.caption: After each review the backlog is re-prioritised using what users have just said.

teach.body: Leila, Head of Member Services, is product owner. She ranks the backlog, and answers developers' questions about how bookings should work. At the end of time box two, the team demonstrates online booking and card payment. Leila accepts booking, but rejects the payment screen because it fails an agreed acceptance criterion. When members ask for a waiting list, she moves it up and drops friend-sharing down, keeping the time box and budget fixed.

teach.h: Time and cost fixed, scope flexes
teach.body: In iterative working, each time box has a fixed end date and fixed resources. If not everything fits, it is the scope that gives way: lower-priority items are deferred. That makes the product owner's prioritisation decisive, because it determines which features are delivered first and which can wait. Value comes first, so the most important features are always the ones that are delivered.

teach.h: Product owner, project manager and sponsor

teach.text: The product owner is NOT the sponsor: the product owner owns the BACKLOG, the sponsor owns the BUSINESS CASE and the funding. Nor does the product owner run the project day to day: that is still the project manager. Watch for other agile job titles used as distractors; the PFQ role that prioritises the backlog is the product owner.

items: Product owner: an iterative-project role representing the business and users.
Owns and prioritises the product backlog, the prioritised list of requirements.
Clarifies requirements for the team and accepts or rejects completed work each iteration.
Aims to maximise value; when a time box is tight, lower-priority scope is deferred.

summary: You can now describe the product owner's role on iterative projects, explain what the product backlog is and how it is prioritised, and distinguish the product owner from the sponsor and the project manager.

A.q: On an iterative project, which role owns the product backlog?
A.why: The product owner owns and prioritises the product backlog.

whyNot.0: The sponsor owns the business case, not the backlog.
whyNot.2: The project manager manages delivery but the backlog belongs to the product owner.
whyNot.3: The PMO supports with standards and reporting; it does not own any project's backlog.

A.q: Whose interests does the product owner represent?
A.why: The product owner represents the business and users, making sure the team builds what delivers most value to them.

whyNot.1: The supplier's interests are represented by a senior supplier on the board.
whyNot.2: The PMO is a support function; the product owner does not speak for it.
whyNot.3: Regulators may set constraints, but the product owner represents the business and its users.

options: A log of the risks and their owners
A list of decision gate dates
A.why: The product backlog is the prioritised list of requirements (features and fixes), with the most valuable at the top.

whyNot.1: Approved changes are recorded through change control and configuration records.
whyNot.2: Gate dates appear in the schedule; the backlog is about requirements.

B.q: At the end of each iteration, who accepts or rejects the completed work?
B.why: The product owner accepts or rejects the work completed in each iteration, on behalf of the business and users.

whyNot.0: The PMO supports projects; it does not accept product features.
whyNot.1: The board makes key decisions and gate approvals, not iteration-by-iteration acceptance.
whyNot.3: The team builds the work; it should not accept its own output on the business's behalf.

B.q: Complete the statement: the product owner's overall aim is to…
B.why: By prioritising the backlog and accepting only work that meets needs, the product owner maximises the value delivered.

whyNot.0: Managing risk is a project manager responsibility, supported by the whole team.
whyNot.1: Standard methods are provided by a PMO.
whyNot.2: Securing funding is the sponsor's job.

B.q: A time box is running out of time. Which decision is the product owner most likely to make?
options: Extend the time box's end date
Add more budget to the time box
B.why: In a time box, time and resources are fixed, so scope flexes: the product owner defers lower-priority items.

whyNot.1: A time box's end date is fixed; that is the point of time boxing.
whyNot.2: Cost and resources are fixed in a time box; scope is what is adjusted.
whyNot.3: Gate approvals are a governance decision, not a product owner one.

C.q: Partway through an iterative project, users ask for a new reporting feature. How is this normally handled?
options: The sponsor rewrites the business case
It joins the backlog and the PO ranks it
The team builds it at once in this time box
The PMO decides whether it is included
C.why: New requirements are added to the backlog and the product owner prioritises them against everything else.

whyNot.0: A single new feature is handled through the backlog; it does not mean rewriting the business case.
whyNot.2: Work in the current time box is already agreed; new items wait to be prioritised.
whyNot.3: The PMO does not decide product scope.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following are product owner responsibilities?
1) Clarifying requirements for the team
2) Chairing the governance board
3) Accepting or rejecting completed work
4) Owning the business case
C.why: The product owner clarifies requirements (1) and accepts or rejects completed work (3).

whyNot.0: Chairing the board (2) is usually the sponsor's role.
whyNot.1: Owning the business case (4) is the sponsor's role.

C.q: Which statement best contrasts the product owner with the project sponsor?
options: PO owns the backlog; sponsor the business case
PO owns the business case; sponsor the backlog
PO funds the project; sponsor accepts the work
PO chairs the board; sponsor clarifies needs
C.why: The product owner owns and prioritises the backlog; the sponsor owns the business case and secures the funding.

whyNot.2: The sponsor secures funding, and the product owner accepts each iteration's work.
whyNot.3: The sponsor usually chairs the board, and clarifying requirements is the product owner's job.

reteach.title: The product owner is the head chef planning the menu
reteach.question: A restaurant is launching a new menu, adding dishes week by week. Who decides which dish the kitchen develops next, and who tastes and approves it?

blocks.body: The head chef knows the diners best, so she keeps a ranked list of dishes to develop: the most popular requests at the top. Each week the cooks develop the top few. On Friday she tastes them: approved dishes go on the menu, the rest go back for more work. If diners start asking for a vegan option, she moves it up the list. The week's length doesn't change; what gets developed does.

blocks.text: The head chef ranks and approves the dishes; the restaurant owner (the sponsor) decides whether the new menu is worth investing in at all.

explain.body: The product owner is the business and user voice within an iterative team, so decisions about what to build reflect real needs and value.

test.q: Why is the product owner usually drawn from the business side?
options: To provide the technical coding skills
To represent users' needs and value
test.why: The product owner represents the business and its users, so they need a business perspective to judge value.

whyNot.0: Technical skills come from the development team.
whyNot.1: Auditing compliance is an assurance activity, often by a PMO or auditors.
whyNot.2: Supplier contracts are managed through procurement and the project manager.

explain.body: The product owner owns the product backlog and keeps it in priority order, often using MoSCoW, so the most valuable items are always at the top.

test.q: Which technique might a product owner use to prioritise backlog items?
test.why: MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't have this time) is a prioritisation technique used on iterative projects.

whyNot.0: PESTLE analyses external factors in the project's environment.
whyNot.2: Tuckman describes stages of team development.

explain.body: During an iteration the product owner answers the team's questions about requirements. At the end, the product owner accepts or rejects the completed work.

test.q: A developer is unsure what a backlog item means. Who should clarify it?
test.why: Clarifying requirements for the team is a product owner responsibility.

whyNot.0: The sponsor works at senior level and does not clarify individual backlog items.
whyNot.1: The PMO supports with methods and reporting, not requirement detail.
whyNot.3: The board makes key decisions; it does not explain individual requirements.

explain.body: In a time box, time and cost are fixed. When work doesn't fit, scope flexes: the product owner defers lower-priority items so the most valuable work is delivered first.

test.q: Which element does the product owner flex to protect value within a time box?
test.why: In a time box the end date and resources are fixed, so scope is adjusted by deferring lower-priority items.

whyNot.1: The time box's end date does not move.
whyNot.2: Cost is fixed per time box in iterative working.
whyNot.3: Resources are fixed for the time box; scope is what changes.
